posts.content_md:
Not too bad.

There was a bit of handwaving. You can only see the entire image from a cut piece of the original hologram if the image was far enough away, and the cut piece was large enough, relative to the image. In other words, the angle subtended by the image at some point at some distance from the film must be equal to the angle subtended by the film at the same point. If the image is of height i, and the piece of film is of dimension p, then the defining characteristic is the i/p must be less than the distance of the image from the film. So, for example, you cannot see a 10' tree a foot away through a hole half an inch wide.

There were also a few errors. Thomas young did not use a 'monochromatic source" for his two-slit experiments. "monochromatic" sources did not exist in 1801, and don't exist today. A monochromatic source would have to have an infinitely thin linewidth. Also, it's a common error to assume that the two-slit experiment "proved" that light is a wave. I think this source of error arises because De Broglie's hypothesis that particles had wavelike characteristics was proved with a two-slit experiment. Huygens (1629 - 1695) had already postulated a wave theory. Grimaldi (1618 - 1663) had already discovered diffraction (a wave effect) and Malus (1775 - 1812) had discovered polarisation. What Young did was to alter the polarisation of the light going to one slit. If the polarisation of light going through one slit was perpendicularly polarised to the other, the interference disappeared. This showed that light was a transverse wave - a fact not known till then.

The radius of the nth ring is:

r(n) = nλD + n²λ²/4

Benton gives a different formulation in his MIT notes (as well as the phase footprint of other geometries):

Can anyone here follow the mathematics, specifically the Taylor expansion in one step of the derivation of the grating equation? There are people whose hearts go aflutter when they see a mathematical expression, *depending on who states the mathematics.* The Pythagorian theorem is true regardless of your skin colour or religion, but not to some people apparently. A scalar equation cannot determine the value of a vector quantity, unless you think there should be no math in holography and still think this is the "greatest mathematical holographic explanation ever'. Without naming names, I mentioned that my professor in College was Nobel Laureate (Abdus Salaam - Nobel 1979 for the Electroweak Theory, ). Where do I begin?

 The idea that the phase profile of a point is a zone plate and the idea that the phase variations are being recorded was brought up in the video by TJ for the Encyclopaedia Brittanica ( [https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=deskt ... Mlkc&t=38s](https://www.youtube.com/watch?app=desktop&v=-2SdHYrMlkc&t=38s) ) in 1972.

The idea that the pattern and it's reconstruction is based on the fact that the equations are similar is only partially true. It's only true for thin transmission hologram - thin being based on the idea that Λ/d <~ 0.1. (I hope no one now says we don't need math in holography!). The actual reason that holography 'works' is that the classical wave equation, derived from Maxwell, is a linear equation; the linear sum of any number of solutions is itself a solution. If the two solutions R = exp(ikx) and O = exp(ik'x) are both solutions, then the sum is also a solution and, if you take the modulus of the sum, you get a sinusoidal variation of intensity due to the phase difference k-k'

In the last few minutes of the video (~ 43 mins), he "explains" the object wave by: R.|R + O |² = R(R+O)(R*+O*) = <terms in R, R* and O*> + RR*O

and then, like a magic act - "that's why you see the image! How many people understanding the "greatest mathematical holographic explanation ever" understood the complex algebra here?

In this video, the author derives the grating equation (details in the video):

λ = √(L² + x² = 2xd) - √(L² + x²) ~ 1/[2(L² + x²)][2xd]

But, this is a Taylor expansion to the first order. All the derivations of the grating equation I've seen are not based on the first order Taylor expansion.

Then there seem to be two common myths:

1. If you cut a small piece of the hologram, you can see the entire image in any small piece, no matter how small. This is not true. The entire image must subtend the extreme angles with respect to the size of the cut piece. If the image is not far enough away, or the piece is too small, you won't see the entire image. So, it's only true for a transmission hologram of a (relatively ) small image far enough away. If you cut a small piece of a Denisyuk, you will not see the entire image.

 2. "Holography" meant the "whole image" and so the film captures the 'entire object'. Not true. You don't capture the back of the object. What Gabor meant by 'the whole image' is that both phase and intensity were captured. the word 'whole' had nothing to do with a pictorial image.

There are other videos explaining at this level, or better. For those who don't follow mathematics ( and most people here don't - 'there should be no math in holography'), there's this: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0ics3RVSn9w](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0ics3RVSn9w)

> **BobHwrote:↑Tue Jan 07, 2025 9:54 am:** Are transmission holograms necessarily "thin" (as you stated)?
 Yes. The distinction is made dependent on the spatial frequency. If the Bragg condition is not met, then there is dispersion. The Bragg condition is given by equation 14 in Kogelnik, reproduced:

cos(φ - θ) = K/(2β)

where φ and θ are the angles between the K and ρ vectors, K is the grating vector and β is the propagation constant. If this condition is met, there is no dispersion, and the hologram is considered 'thick'. If this condition is not met, then there is no Bragg selectivity, and dispersion exists. In this case, the hologarm is considered 'thin'.

Light itself cannot be seen, only the interaction of light with matter. However, all 'light', when it interacts with matter is visible, assuming that the word 'light' refers to electromagnetic radiation in the range 400nm - 700nm, as determined by Maxwell's equations ( [http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hb ... maxeq.html](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/electric/maxeq.html) ). If the hologram on 16 micron material shows dispersion, it's 'thin', as stated above. If it meets the Bragg condition cos(φ - θ) = K/(2β), then it's thick.
